questions.question: The chapter's epigraph says a system cannot be successful if it is too strongly influenced by a single person, and that the real test begins once people with many different viewpoints undertake their own experiments. Who is it attributed to, and what is it doing at the head of a batch-processing chapter?

options.text: Donald Knuth — it frames the chapter's themes of composability and experimentation, which the Unix philosophy makes concrete with 'expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program'
Doug McIlroy — it introduces the invention of pipes
Jeff Dean — it introduces MapReduce
Eric Raymond — it introduces The Art of UNIX Programming

questions.explanation: Many viewpoints running their own experiments is exactly what composable tools enable.

questions.question: What style of data processing do Parts I and II assume, and which systems work that way?

options.text: Requests and queries, and the corresponding responses or results — you ask for something or send an instruction, and some time later the system hopefully gives you an answer. This is how databases, caches, search indexes, web servers and many other systems work
Batch jobs scheduled nightly, as in data warehouses
Streams of events processed continuously
Peer-to-peer gossip between nodes

questions.explanation: Request/response is so ingrained it's easy to take for granted — but it is not the only way of building systems.

questions.question: What does the chapter say we generally assume about a request in an online system?

options.text: That it is triggered by a human user, and that the user is waiting for the response — so they shouldn't have to wait too long, which is why we pay a lot of attention to the response time of these systems
That it is triggered by another machine and nobody is waiting
That it is idempotent and can be retried freely
That it touches only one partition

questions.explanation: A waiting human is what makes response time the governing metric.

questions.question: Match the three system types to their primary performance measure. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Services (online systems) wait for a request or instruction to arrive and try to handle it as quickly as possible, sending a response back; response time is usually the primary measure of performance, and availability is often very important — if the client can't reach the service, the user will probably get an error message

Batch processing systems (offline systems) take a large amount of input data, run a job to process it, and produce some output data; the primary performance measure is usually throughput — the time it takes to crunch through an input dataset of a certain size

Stream processing systems (near-real-time systems) consume inputs and produce outputs rather than responding to requests; a stream job operates on events shortly after they happen, which allows lower latency than the equivalent batch systems
All three are measured primarily by availability

questions.explanation: Response time, throughput, and latency respectively.

questions.question: How long do batch jobs take, and how are they started?

options.text: Jobs often take a while — from a few minutes to several days — so there normally isn't a user waiting for the job to finish; instead batch jobs are often scheduled to run periodically, for example once a day
Jobs take seconds and are triggered by user requests
Jobs take hours and are triggered by incoming events
Jobs run continuously with no scheduling

questions.explanation: Minutes to days, on a periodic schedule, with nobody waiting.

questions.question: On what property does the chapter draw the stream/batch line?

options.text: On the boundedness of the input: a stream job operates on events shortly after they happen, whereas a batch job operates on a fixed set of input data. This difference allows stream processing systems to have lower latency than the equivalent batch systems — which is why stream processing is called near-real-time or nearline, and is deferred to Chapter 11
On latency alone, which is the defining difference
On whether the data is in HDFS or in a queue
On whether the job is scheduled or continuous

questions.explanation: Boundedness, not latency, is the structural distinction — latency is a consequence. Chapter 11 builds upon batch processing.

questions.question: When was MapReduce published, what was it called, and where was it implemented?

options.text: Published in 2004, and subsequently — perhaps overenthusiastically — called 'the algorithm that makes Google so massively scalable'. It was subsequently implemented in various open source data systems, including Hadoop, CouchDB and MongoDB
Published in 1998, called 'the Google File System', implemented in HDFS
Published in 2008, called 'the Hadoop algorithm', implemented in Spark and Flink
Published in 2004, called 'bulk synchronous parallel', implemented in Pregel

questions.explanation: 2004, with the overenthusiastic label the chapter quotes from The Perils of JavaSchools.

questions.question: What was MapReduce's actual novelty, and why is it still worth studying?

options.text: It was not novel as a programming model — it is a fairly low-level programming model compared to the parallel processing systems developed for data warehouses many years previously — but it was a major step forward in terms of the scale of processing that could be achieved on commodity hardware. Although its importance is now declining, it is still worth understanding because it provides a clear picture of why and how batch processing is useful
It was novel as a programming model and remains the state of the art
It was novel in neither respect and is no longer worth studying
It was novel in its query language, which is still widely used

questions.explanation: Scale on commodity hardware, not conceptual novelty.

questions.question: What historical examples of batch processing does the chapter give?

options.text: Punch card tabulating machines such as the Hollerith machines used in the 1890 US Census, which implemented a semi-mechanized form of batch processing to compute aggregate statistics from large inputs; and electromechanical IBM card-sorting machines, widely used for business data processing in the 1940s and 1950s. The programs for these machines bear an uncanny resemblance to MapReduce — as usual, history has a tendency of repeating itself
The ENIAC in 1945 and the IBM 360 in 1964
Punched tape systems from the 1920s only
There are no pre-computer examples

questions.explanation: 1890 to 2004 is 114 years; the 1978 statement of the Unix philosophy to the 2004 MapReduce paper is 26 years — and the chapter says surprisingly little has changed in four decades.

questions.question: What does the example nginx log line tell us? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That the request was made on February 27, 2015, at 17:55:11 UTC, for the file /css/typography.css, from the client IP address 216.58.210.78
That the user was not authenticated, so the remote_user field is set to a hyphen
That the response status was 200, meaning the request was successful, and the response was 3,377 bytes in size
That the web browser was Chrome 40, and it loaded the file because it was referenced in the page at the URL http://martin.kleppmann.com/

questions.explanation: There's a lot of information in one line — to interpret it you need to look at the definition of the log format. The example posits a web server that appends a line to a log file every time it serves a request, which makes the log append-only, immutable and bounded.

questions.question: In the Unix pipeline for finding the five most popular pages, what does 'awk {print $7}' do?

options.text: It splits each line into fields by whitespace and outputs only the seventh such field, which is the requested URL
It prints the seventh line of the file
It prints the seventh character of each line
It counts seven fields and discards the rest

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that some people love to point out that cat is unnecessary here, since the input file could be given directly as an argument to awk — but the linear pipeline is more apparent when written like this. The seventh whitespace-separated field lands on the URL because the request field is quoted and splits into three whitespace fields.

questions.question: The first sort produces no counts and no ranking. Why is it there?

options.text: Because it alphabetically sorts the list of requested URLs, so if some URL has been requested n times, after sorting the file contains the same URL repeated n times in a row — which is exactly what uniq needs, since it filters out repeated lines by checking whether two adjacent lines are the same
Because head requires sorted input
Because awk outputs fields in random order
It is unnecessary and could be removed

questions.explanation: Adjacency is what makes counting possible without a hash table. This sort step is implicit in MapReduce.

questions.question: What do 'uniq -c' and 'sort -r -n' each do?

options.text: uniq filters out repeated lines in its input by checking whether two adjacent lines are the same, and the -c option additionally outputs a counter — for every distinct URL, how many times that URL appeared in the input. The second sort sorts by the number (-n) at the start of each line, which is the number of times the URL was requested, in reverse (-r) order, meaning largest number first
uniq removes duplicates without counting; sort -r -n sorts alphabetically in reverse
uniq counts all lines; sort -r -n sorts by URL numerically
uniq sorts and counts; sort -r -n reverses the file

questions.explanation: Each program does one thing well. Finally head outputs just the first five lines (-n 5) of input and discards the rest, giving the top five pages.

questions.question: The output shows 4189 /favicon.ico, 3631 for an SSH keys article, 2124 for a schema evolution article, 1369 for /, and 915 for /css/typography.css. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The top five URLs account for 12,228 requests in total
The single most-requested URL accounts for about 34% of that total
The top entry, /favicon.ico, is arguably not a 'page' at all — it is the browser's tab icon
The top five URLs account for about 8,000 requests

questions.question: You are asked to omit CSS files from the report, and separately to rank client IP addresses rather than pages. What changes?

options.text: Only the awk stage changes — for example changing the awk argument to '$7 !~ /\.css$/ {print $7}' to omit CSS files, or to '{print $1}' to rank client IP addresses. Since you can easily modify the analysis to suit your needs, it is incredibly powerful, and it will process gigabytes of log files in a matter of seconds
The entire pipeline must be rewritten for each variation
The sort stage changes in the first case and head in the second
Neither variation is possible with these tools

questions.explanation: One stage changes; the rest of the pipeline is untouched.

questions.question: Which Unix tools does the chapter recommend learning, and what claim does it cite?

options.text: awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq and xargs — surprisingly many data analyses can be done in a few minutes using some combination of these, and they perform surprisingly well, citing Adam Drake's 'Command-Line Tools Can Be 235x Faster than Your Hadoop Cluster'
find, xargs and tar, citing the POSIX standard
python, perl and ruby, citing benchmark studies
hadoop, hive and pig, citing Google's paper

questions.explanation: Six tools, with a real performance claim behind them.

questions.question: The chapter offers a Ruby program as an alternative to the pipeline. What does it maintain, and why does the array index differ from awk's field number?

options.text: It maintains a hash table of counters, zero by default; from each log line it takes the URL to be the seventh whitespace-separated field, with array index 6 because Ruby's arrays are zero-indexed — so $7 and [6] refer to the same field. It then increments the counter for that URL, sorts the hash table contents by counter value descending, takes the top five entries, and prints them
It maintains a sorted array; the indices differ because the log format differs
It maintains a database connection; the indices genuinely refer to different fields
It maintains no state; the index is arbitrary

questions.explanation: Same field, different indexing convention — a purely syntactic difference.

questions.question: What actually differs between the pipeline and the Ruby script?

options.text: The difference is not just superficial syntactic differences — there is a big difference in the execution flow, which becomes apparent if you run this analysis on a large file. On readability the chapter refuses to pick a winner: which of the two you prefer is partly a matter of taste
Only syntax differs; execution is identical
The Ruby version is always faster
The pipeline is always more readable

questions.explanation: Execution flow, not syntax, is what matters at scale.

questions.question: What do the Ruby script and the Unix pipeline each keep in memory, and what decides which is better?

options.text: The Ruby script keeps an in-memory hash table of URLs, where each URL is mapped to the number of times it has been seen. The Unix pipeline does not have such a hash table, but instead relies on sorting a list of URLs in which multiple occurrences of the same URL are simply repeated. Which approach is better? It depends how many different URLs you have
Both keep hash tables; the difference is the hash function
Both sort; the difference is the sort algorithm
Neither keeps state in memory

questions.explanation: Hash table versus sorted repetition, decided by cardinality.

questions.question: Define working set, and what memory budget suffices for most small to mid-sized websites?

options.text: The working set is the amount of memory to which the job needs random access. For a log with a million entries for a single URL, the space required in the hash table is still just one URL plus the size of the counter — so the size of the working set depends only on the number of distinct URLs. For most small to mid-sized websites you can probably fit all distinct URLs, and a counter for each, in say 1 GB of memory, in which case an in-memory hash table works fine, even on a laptop
The working set is the total input size; 1 TB is needed
The working set is the number of log lines; 1 GB per million lines is needed
The working set is the output size; no memory is needed

questions.explanation: Distinct keys, not total records, determine the working set.

questions.question: When the working set exceeds available memory, why does sorting win?

options.text: Because the sorting approach can make efficient use of disks: chunks of data can be sorted in memory and written out to disk as segment files, and then multiple sorted segments can be merged into a larger sorted file — the same principle as SSTables and LSM-trees. Mergesort has sequential access patterns that perform well on disks, and optimizing for sequential I/O was a recurring theme in Chapter 3
Because sorting uses less CPU than hashing
Because sorting requires no disk at all
Because hash tables cannot be spilled to disk in any implementation

questions.explanation: The GNU Coreutils sort utility on Linux automatically handles larger-than-memory datasets by spilling to disk, and automatically parallelizes sorting across multiple CPU cores — so it easily scales to large datasets without running out of memory, and the bottleneck becomes the rate at which the input file can be read from disk.

questions.question: Who invented Unix pipes, when, and with what analogy?

options.text: Doug McIlroy, who first described them in 1964: 'We should have some ways of connecting programs like garden hose — screw in another segment when it becomes necessary to massage data in another way. This is the way of I/O also.' The plumbing analogy stuck, and the idea became part of what is now known as the Unix philosophy
Ken Thompson in 1970, with a plumbing analogy
Dennis Ritchie in 1978, with an assembly-line analogy
Eric Raymond in 1999, with a Lego analogy

questions.explanation: 1964 for the description, with the garden-hose image that gave pipes their name.

questions.question: Which are the four principles of the Unix philosophy as published in 1978? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new 'features'

Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program. Don't clutter output with extraneous information, avoid stringently columnar or binary input formats, and don't insist on interactive input
Design and build software, even operating systems, to be tried early, ideally within weeks. Don't hesitate to throw away the clumsy parts and rebuild them
Use tools in preference to unskilled help to lighten a programming task, even if you have to detour to build the tools and expect to throw some of them out after you've finished using them

questions.explanation: Principles 1 and 2 are the ones the Summary carries forward into MapReduce.

questions.question: What five properties does the chapter name, and what does it compare them to?

options.text: Automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration, being friendly to experimentation, and breaking down large projects into manageable chunks — which sounds remarkably like the Agile and DevOps movements of today. Surprisingly little has changed in four decades
Reliability, scalability, maintainability, security and compliance — compared to Chapter 1's concerns
Speed, cost, simplicity, safety and portability — compared to the cloud
The five properties are unnamed

questions.explanation: A 1978 philosophy that prefigures Agile and DevOps.

questions.question: Why is sort the chapter's exemplar, and what is the sting in the tail?

options.text: Because it is arguably a better sorting implementation than most programming languages have in their standard libraries, which do not spill to disk and do not use multiple threads even when that would be beneficial. And yet sort is barely useful in isolation: it only becomes powerful in combination with the other Unix tools such as uniq — which raises the question, what does Unix do to enable this composability?
Because it is the fastest tool, and there is no sting
Because it is the simplest tool, and the sting is that it is slow
Because it does many things, and the sting is that it violates the philosophy

questions.explanation: A shell like bash lets us easily compose these small programs into surprisingly powerful data processing jobs, even though many of them are written by different groups of people.

questions.question: What is the uniform interface in Unix, precisely?

options.text: A file, or more precisely a file descriptor. A file is just an ordered sequence of bytes — and because that is such a simple interface, many different things can be represented using the same interface: an actual file on the filesystem, a communication channel to another process (a Unix socket, stdin, stdout), a device driver, a socket representing a TCP connection, and so on. If you want to be able to connect any program's output to any program's input, that means all programs must use the same input/output interface
A record, defined as a tuple of typed fields
A stream of structured objects
A pipe, which is distinct from a file

questions.explanation: A footnote gives a second example: URLs and HTTP, the foundations of the web. A URL identifies a particular resource on a website, and you can link to any URL from any other website, so users can seamlessly jump between websites by following links even though the servers may be operated by entirely unrelated organizations — a key insight in making the web the success that it is. The pre-web counter-example is bulletin board systems, each with its own phone number and baud rate configuration: to reference content on a different BBS you had to hang up, dial the other BBS, and manually find the information, since it wasn't possible to link directly to content inside another BBS.

questions.question: Which record separator do the example tools agree on, and what would arguably have been better?

options.text: awk, sort, uniq and head all treat their input file as a list of records separated by the newline character, ASCII 0x0A. The choice of newline is arbitrary — arguably the ASCII record separator 0x1E would have been a better choice since it's intended for this purpose — but in any case, the fact that all these programs have standardized on using the same record separator allows them to interoperate
They agree on the tab character; the comma would have been better
They agree on 0x1E already, which is ideal
There is no agreed separator

questions.explanation: Record separation is standardized; record parsing is more vague — some tools assume whitespace or tab separation, others use CSV, pipe-separated or other encodings, and even something as simple as quoting has half a dozen command-line options in xargs.

questions.question: What is the chapter's own complaint about ASCII text as a uniform interface?

options.text: It's not exactly beautiful: having to write something like {print $7} to extract the URL is not very readable — in an ideal world this would perhaps be {print $request_url} or something of that sort. The chapter says it will return to this idea later, and it does: most Unix tools assume untyped text files, so more structured file formats such as Avro and Parquet eliminate these low-value syntactic conversions
It is too slow to parse
It cannot represent binary data at all
There is no complaint; the chapter praises it unreservedly

questions.explanation: Positional field references are the cost of an untyped interface.

questions.question: How rare is Unix-grade composability today?

options.text: Today it's an exception, not the norm, to have programs that work together as smoothly as Unix tools do: you can't easily pipe the contents of your email account and your online shopping history through a custom analysis tool into a spreadsheet and post the results to a social network or a wiki. Even databases with the same data model often don't make it easy to get data out of one and into the other, and this lack of integration leads to Balkanization of data
It is the norm; most modern tools compose as well as Unix tools
It is universal within cloud platforms
It has improved steadily since 1978

questions.explanation: Balkanization of data is the term for the resulting state of affairs.

questions.question: What are stdin and stdout bound to by default, and what can change the wiring?

options.text: If you run a program and don't specify anything else, stdin comes from the keyboard and stdout goes to the screen. However you can also take input from a file, redirect output to a file, or use pipes to attach the stdout of one process to the stdin of another process — with a small in-memory buffer, and without writing the entire intermediate data stream to disk
Both are bound to files by default; only pipes can change this
Both are bound to the network by default
They cannot be rebound

questions.explanation: Pipes stream through a small buffer rather than materializing intermediate state — which is exactly what MapReduce does differently.

questions.question: What three existing names does the chapter offer for a program not knowing where its input comes from?

options.text: Loose coupling, late binding (Alan Kay) or inversion of control (Martin Fowler). Separating the input/output wiring from the program logic makes it easier to compose small tools into bigger systems — a program can still read and write files directly if it needs to, but the Unix approach works best if a program doesn't worry about particular file paths and simply uses stdin and stdout
Encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism
Dependency injection, service location and reflection
Modularity, cohesion and coupling

questions.explanation: Three existing names for one property, from three different traditions.

questions.question: You want to add stages that translate user-agent strings into browser identifiers and IP addresses into country codes. What must your programs do, and what does sort need to know about them?

options.text: Your program just needs to read input from stdin and write output to stdout, and it can participate in data processing pipelines. What sort needs to know about your program: nothing. It doesn't care whether it's communicating with another part of the operating system or with a program written by you
Your program must register with sort and declare its schema
Your program must be written in C and linked against sort
Your program must implement a plugin interface

questions.explanation: Two file descriptors are the whole contract.

questions.question: What limits does the chapter put on stdin/stdout wiring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Programs that need multiple inputs or outputs are possible but tricky
You can't pipe a program's output into a network connection

If a program directly opens files for reading and writing, or starts another program as a subprocess, or opens a network connection, then that I/O is wired up by the program itself — it can still be configurable via command-line options, but the flexibility of wiring up inputs and outputs in a shell is reduced
Programs cannot read from files at all

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that except by using a separate tool such as netcat or curl, and that Unix started out trying to represent everything as files but the BSD sockets API deviated from that convention — the research operating systems Plan 9 and Inferno are more consistent in their use of files, representing a TCP connection as a file in /net/tcp.

questions.question: Why do Unix tools make it easy to see what is going on? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The input files to Unix commands are normally treated as immutable, so you can run the commands as often as you want, trying various command-line options, without damaging the input files
You can end the pipeline at any point, pipe the output into less, and look at it to see if it has the expected form — this ability to inspect is great for debugging
You can write the output of one pipeline stage to a file and use that file as input to the next stage, which lets you restart the later stage without rerunning the entire pipeline
They include a query optimizer that explains the plan

questions.explanation: So even though Unix tools are quite blunt, simple tools compared to a query optimizer of a relational database, they remain amazingly useful, especially for experimentation.

questions.question: What does the chapter name as the biggest limitation of Unix tools?

options.text: That they run only on a single machine — and that's where tools like Hadoop come in
That they only handle text, not binary data
That they cannot be scripted
That they have no fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Single-machine execution is the one limitation Hadoop exists to remove.

questions.question: Complete and defend the chapter's analogy: MapReduce is a bit like Unix tools, but…

options.text: …distributed across potentially thousands of machines. Like Unix tools it is a fairly blunt, brute-force, but surprisingly effective tool. A single MapReduce job is comparable to a single Unix process: it takes one or more inputs and produces one or more outputs. So Hadoop is somewhat like a distributed version of Unix, where HDFS is the filesystem and MapReduce is a quirky implementation of a Unix process
…with a declarative query language instead of shell commands
…running on a single very large machine
…operating on streams rather than files

questions.explanation: A job is a process; HDFS is the filesystem.

questions.question: What two Unix-like restraints does a MapReduce job observe?

options.text: Running a MapReduce job normally does not modify the input and does not have any side effects other than producing the output. The output files are written once, in a sequential fashion, not modifying any existing part of a file once it has been written
It modifies the input in place and appends to existing outputs
It may have arbitrary side effects but must not modify the input
It may modify the input but must have no side effects

questions.explanation: Immutable input, write-once output.

questions.question: What do MapReduce jobs use instead of stdin and stdout, and what is Hadoop's implementation?

options.text: MapReduce jobs read and write files on a distributed filesystem. In Hadoop's implementation of MapReduce that filesystem is called HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System, an open source reimplementation of the Google File System (GFS) described in the 2003 paper by Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff and Shun-Tak Leung
They use TCP sockets; the implementation is YARN
They use local disks; the implementation is ext4
They use a message queue; the implementation is Kafka

questions.explanation: Files and pipes are substituted by a distributed filesystem — the key structural claim.

questions.question: Which alternative storage systems does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Other distributed filesystems besides HDFS, such as GlusterFS and the Quantcast File System (QFS)
Object storage services such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage and OpenStack Swift, which are similar in many ways
The chapter mostly uses HDFS as a running example, but the principles apply to any distributed filesystem
Relational databases such as PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: A footnote names one real difference: with HDFS, computing tasks can be scheduled to run on the machine that stores a copy of a particular file, whereas object stores usually keep storage and computation separate. Reading from a local disk has a performance advantage if network bandwidth is a bottleneck — but note that if erasure coding is used, the locality advantage is lost, because the data from several machines must be combined in order to reconstitute the original file.

questions.question: Which principle is HDFS based on, and what does it contrast with?

options.text: The shared-nothing principle, in contrast to the shared-disk approach of Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Storage Area Network (SAN) architectures. Shared-disk storage is implemented by a centralized storage appliance, often using custom hardware and special network infrastructure such as Fibre Channel, whereas the shared-nothing approach requires no special hardware, only computers connected by a conventional datacenter network
The shared-disk principle, in contrast to shared-nothing
The shared-memory principle, in contrast to message passing
The shared-everything principle, in contrast to partitioning

questions.explanation: Commodity hardware on a conventional network is the whole point.

questions.question: How is HDFS put together?

options.text: It consists of a daemon process running on each machine, exposing a network service that allows other nodes to access files stored on that machine — assuming every general-purpose machine in a datacenter has some disks attached to it — plus a central server called the NameNode that keeps track of which file blocks are stored on which machine. Thus HDFS conceptually creates one big filesystem that can use the space on the disks of all machines running the daemon
It consists of a single storage server with attached disks
It consists of daemons only, with no central metadata server
It consists of a NameNode only, with data stored in S3

questions.explanation: Per-machine daemons plus a central block map.

questions.question: How does HDFS survive machine and disk failure?

options.text: File blocks are replicated on multiple machines — either simply several copies of the same data on multiple machines as in Chapter 5, or an erasure coding scheme such as Reed–Solomon codes which allows lost data to be recovered with lower storage overhead than full replication. The techniques are similar to RAID, which provides redundancy across several disks attached to the same machine — the difference being that in a distributed filesystem, file access and replication are done over a conventional datacenter network without special hardware
It relies on RAID within each machine only
It relies on nightly backups to tape
It does not tolerate disk failure

questions.explanation: At the time of writing, the biggest HDFS deployments run on tens of thousands of machines with combined storage capacity of hundreds of petabytes — viable because the cost of data storage and access on HDFS, using commodity hardware and open source software, is much lower than that of the equivalent capacity on a dedicated storage appliance.

questions.question: State MapReduce's four-step pattern and its log-analysis counterparts. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Read a set of input files and break it up into records — in the web server log example, each record is one line in the log, so the newline is the record separator
Call the mapper function to extract a key and value from each input record — here the mapper function is awk {print $7}: it extracts the URL as the key and leaves the value empty
Sort all of the key-value pairs by key — in the log example this is done by the first sort command
Call the reducer function to iterate over the sorted key-value pairs — here the reducer is implemented by uniq -c, which counts the number of adjacent records with the same key

questions.explanation: Four steps, mapping exactly onto the four pipeline stages.

questions.question: Of the four steps, which do you write and which does the framework supply?

options.text: Steps 2 (map) and 4 (reduce) are where you write your custom data processing code. Step 1, breaking files into records, is handled by the input format parser. Step 3, the sort step, is implicit in MapReduce — you don't have to write it, because the output from the mapper is always sorted before it is given to the reducer
You write all four steps
You write only step 3; the framework supplies the rest
The framework supplies all four steps

questions.explanation: This is why the chapter calls MapReduce a quirky implementation of a Unix process which happens to always run the sort utility between the map phase and the reduce phase — unconditionally, whereas dataflow engines later make sorting opt-in, needed only where it is actually required.

questions.question: State the mapper's contract in full.

options.text: The mapper is called once for every input record, and its job is to extract the key and value from the input record. For each input it may generate any number of key-value pairs, including none. It does not keep any state from one input record to the next, so each record is handled independently
It is called once per file and maintains state across records
It must generate exactly one key-value pair per record
It is called once per key and receives all matching records

questions.explanation: Statelessness per record is what makes mappers freely parallelizable.

questions.question: State the reducer's contract.

options.text: The MapReduce framework takes the key-value pairs produced by the mappers, collects all the values belonging to the same key, and calls the reducer with an iterator over that collection of values. The reducer can produce output records. Note it is an iterator, not a list — it incrementally scans over all records with the same key, which may in some cases not all fit in memory
It receives one key-value pair at a time with no grouping
It receives a fully materialized list of all values for a key
It receives the entire dataset and must group it itself

questions.explanation: An iterator rather than a list is what lets a key's value set exceed memory.

questions.question: The log pipeline had a second sort. How do you get that in MapReduce?

options.text: By writing a second MapReduce job and using the output of the first job as input to the second job. Thus the role of the mapper is to prepare the data by putting it into a form that is suitable for sorting, and the role of the reducer is to process the data that has been sorted. So one job could determine the number of page views per URL, but not the most popular URLs, since that requires a second round of sorting
By calling sort inside the reducer
By configuring the framework to sort twice
A second sort is impossible in MapReduce

questions.explanation: One sort per job, so a second sort means a second job.

questions.question: What does MapReduce add over a Unix pipeline, and what makes it possible?

options.text: MapReduce can parallelize a computation across many machines, without you having to write code to explicitly handle the parallelism. This is possible because the mapper and reducer only operate on one record at a time, so they don't need to know where their input is coming from or their output is going to — the framework can handle the complexities of moving data between machines
It adds a declarative query language
It adds transactions across machines
It adds low-latency responses

questions.explanation: This is the Unix separation of logic and wiring, applied across a cluster.

questions.question: What are mappers and reducers actually written in?

options.text: It is possible to use standard Unix tools as mappers and reducers in a distributed computation, but more commonly they are implemented as functions in a conventional programming language: in Hadoop MapReduce the mapper and reducer are each a Java class that implements a particular interface, while in MongoDB and CouchDB mappers and reducers are JavaScript functions
Only Unix tools can be used
Only SQL can be used
Only C++ can be used, as at Google

questions.explanation: The chapter cites Manta: Unix Meets Map Reduce for the shell-tool approach.

questions.question: What determines the map-side parallelism, and what does the scheduler try to do?

options.text: The input to a MapReduce job is typically a directory in HDFS, and each file or file block within the input directory is considered to be a separate partition that can be processed by a separate map task — so the parallelism is not chosen by you. Each input file is typically hundreds of megabytes in size, and the MapReduce scheduler tries to run each mapper on one of the machines that stores a replica of the input file, provided that machine has enough spare RAM and CPU resources to run the map task. This principle is known as putting the computation near the data, and it saves copying the input file over the network, reducing network load and increasing locality
You choose the number of mappers, and the scheduler places them randomly
The number of mappers equals the number of machines, and data is copied to them
One mapper per input record, placed by hash

questions.explanation: In most cases the application code that should run in the map task is not yet present on the machine assigned the job, so the MapReduce framework first copies the code — for example JAR files in the case of a Java program — to the appropriate machines. It then starts the map task and begins reading the input file, passing one record at a time to the mapper callback, whose output consists of key-value pairs.

questions.question: Contrast how the numbers of map and reduce tasks are determined, and how a key reaches a reducer.

options.text: The number of map tasks is determined by the number of input file blocks, whereas the number of reduce tasks is configured by the job author and can be different from the number of map tasks. To ensure that all key-value pairs with the same key end up at the same reducer, the framework uses a hash of the key to determine which reduce task should receive a particular key-value pair
Both are configured by the job author
Both are determined by the input block count
Keys reach reducers by range partitioning, not hashing

questions.explanation: Blocks determine mappers; the author determines reducers; hashing routes keys.

questions.question: Why does the sort happen in stages, and where does mapper output go?

options.text: Because the dataset is likely too large to be sorted with a conventional sorting algorithm on a single machine, the sorting is performed in stages: each map task partitions its output by reducer based on the hash of the key, and each of these partitions is written to a sorted file on the mapper's local disk, using a technique similar to SSTables and LSM-trees. Note this is local disk, not HDFS — the chapter later observes that mapper output is intermediate state, and that dataflow engines generalize the idea to all intermediate state
Mapper output goes straight to HDFS, sorted globally in one pass
Mapper output is kept entirely in memory
Mapper output is sorted by the reducers, not the mappers

questions.explanation: Per-mapper sorted partitions on local disk, merged later by reducers.

questions.question: Define the shuffle, and state the chapter's complaint about the name.

options.text: Whenever a mapper finishes reading its input file and writing its sorted output files, the MapReduce scheduler notifies the reducers that they can start fetching the output files from that mapper. The reducers connect to each of the mappers and download the files of sorted key-value pairs for their partition. The process of partitioning by reducer, sorting, and copying data partitions from mappers to reducers is known as the shuffle — a confusing term, because unlike shuffling a deck of cards there is no randomness in MapReduce
The shuffle is the random reassignment of keys to reducers; the name is apt
The shuffle is the sorting step only; the name is apt
The shuffle is the reduce phase; the chapter has no complaint

questions.explanation: Partition, sort and copy — deterministic throughout, despite the name.

questions.question: Describe the reduce side from fetched files to written output.

options.text: The reduce task takes the files from the mappers and merges them together, preserving the sort order — so if different mappers produced records with the same key, they will be adjacent in the merged reducer input. The reducer is called with a key and an iterator that incrementally scans over all records with the same key, which may in some cases not all fit in memory. The reducer can use arbitrary logic to process these records and can generate any number of output records, which are written to a file on the distributed filesystem — usually one copy on the local disk of the machine running the reducer, with replicas on other machines
The reducer sorts the fetched files itself before processing
The reducer writes output to its local disk only, with no replication
The reducer receives unsorted records and must group them in memory

questions.explanation: Merge preserving order, then one reducer call per key.

questions.question: Why is a single MapReduce job usually not enough, and how are jobs chained?

options.text: The range of problems you can solve with a single job is limited — the log example could determine the number of page views per URL but not the most popular URLs, since that requires a second round of sorting. So jobs are chained together into workflows, such that the output of one job becomes the input to the next. Hadoop MapReduce does not have any particular support for workflows, so this chaining is done implicitly by directory name: you configure the first job to write its output to a designated directory in HDFS, and the second job to read that same directory name as its input. From the MapReduce framework's point of view, they are two independent jobs
Jobs are chained by an explicit workflow API in Hadoop MapReduce
Jobs are chained through in-memory pipes
Jobs cannot be chained

questions.explanation: Directory names are the entire chaining mechanism — chained jobs are less like pipelines of Unix commands, which pass output as input directly using only a small in-memory buffer, and more like a sequence of commands where each command's output is written to a temporary file and the next command reads from that file.

questions.question: When is a batch job's output valid, and who enforces workflow dependencies?

options.text: A batch job's output is only considered valid when the job has completed successfully — MapReduce discards the partial output of a failed job. So one job in a workflow can only start when the prior jobs, that is the jobs that produce its input directories, have completed successfully. To handle these dependencies between job executions, various workflow schedulers for Hadoop have been developed, including Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, Airflow and Pinball
Partial output is valid; jobs may start as soon as any input appears
The MapReduce framework enforces dependencies internally
HDFS enforces dependencies through file locks

questions.explanation: All-or-nothing output, with an external scheduler enforcing ordering.

questions.question: How big do workflows get, and which higher-level tools wire them automatically?

options.text: Workflows consisting of 50 to 100 MapReduce jobs are common when building recommendation systems, and in a large organization many different teams may be running different jobs that read each other's output — so tool support is important for managing such complex dataflows. Various higher-level tools for Hadoop have been developed, including Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch and FlumeJava, which also set up workflows of multiple MapReduce stages that are automatically wired together appropriately
Workflows rarely exceed 5 jobs; no tooling is needed
Workflows reach thousands of jobs; only Oozie can manage them
Workflows are always single jobs in practice

questions.explanation: 50 to 100 jobs, with cross-team dependencies — hence the tooling.

questions.question: When is a join necessary, and what does denormalization do about it?

options.text: It is common for records in one dataset to have an association with records in another dataset: a foreign key in a relational model, a document reference in a document model, or an edge in a graph model. A join is necessary whenever you have some code that needs to access records on both sides of that association. Denormalization can reduce the need for joins but generally not remove it entirely
A join is necessary only in relational models; denormalization removes it entirely
A join is never necessary in batch processing
A join is necessary only for graph data; denormalization is irrelevant

questions.explanation: A footnote restricts the chapter's discussion to equi-joins, the most common type of join in which a record is associated with other records that have an identical value in a particular field — some databases support more general types of joins, for example using a less-than operator instead of an equality operator.

questions.question: What does MapReduce do instead of using indexes, and when is that reasonable?

options.text: MapReduce has no concept of indexes, at least not in the usual sense: when given a set of files as input it reads the entire content of all of those files — a database would call this operation a full table scan. If you only want to read a small number of records, a full table scan is outrageously expensive compared to an index lookup. However, in analytic queries it is common to want to calculate aggregates over a large number of records, in which case scanning the entire input might be quite a reasonable thing to do, especially if you can parallelize the processing across multiple machines
MapReduce builds indexes on the fly for each join
MapReduce uses HDFS indexes, which are always faster than scans
MapReduce refuses joins entirely

questions.explanation: In a batch context, join means resolving all occurrences of some association within a dataset — the data for all users simultaneously, not merely looking up the data for one particular user, which would be done far more efficiently with an index.

questions.question: Describe the two datasets in Figure 10-2 and how the example maps onto a star schema.

options.text: On the left is a log of events describing the things that logged-in users did on a website — called activity events or clickstream data — and on the right is a database of users. In star schema terms, the log of events is the fact table and the user database is one of the dimensions. The analytics task might be to correlate user activity with user profile information such as age or date of birth, for example to find which pages are most popular with which age groups. A join is needed because the activity events contain only the user ID, not the full user profile information — embedding that profile information in every single activity event would most likely be too wasteful
Two fact tables joined on a timestamp
Two dimension tables joined on a surrogate key
A single denormalized table requiring no join

questions.explanation: Fact table plus dimension, joined on user ID.

questions.question: Why would querying the user database for every event perform poorly? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The processing throughput would be limited by the round-trip time to the database server
The effectiveness of a local cache would depend very much on the distribution of data
Running a large number of queries in parallel could easily overwhelm the database
The database would refuse concurrent connections

questions.explanation: It is possible, but it would most likely suffer from very poor performance. Two rules follow: in order to achieve good throughput in a batch process, the computation must be local to one machine as much as possible — making random-access requests over the network for every record you want to process is too slow. And querying a remote database would mean the batch job becomes nondeterministic, because the data in the remote database might change.

questions.question: What is the better approach to the join, and where does the copy go?

options.text: Take a copy of the user database — for example extracted from a database backup using an ETL process — and put it in the same distributed filesystem as the log of user activity events. Then you would have the user database in one set of files in HDFS and the user activity records in another set of files, and you can use MapReduce to bring together all of the relevant records in the same place and process them efficiently
Query the live database from the reducer rather than the mapper
Replicate the activity log into the database
Cache the user database in each mapper's memory from the network

questions.explanation: Both sides in HDFS, joined by the framework.

questions.question: In the reduce-side sort-merge join, what does each set of mappers emit?

options.text: One set of mappers goes over the activity events, extracting the user ID as the key and the activity event as the value; another set of mappers goes over the user database, extracting the user ID as the key and the user's date of birth as the value. If the input datasets are partitioned into multiple files, each could be processed with multiple mappers in parallel. The effect is that all the activity events and the user record with the same user ID become adjacent to each other in the reducer input
Both sets emit the event timestamp as the key
Only the activity mappers emit; the user database is loaded into memory
Both sets emit the date of birth as the key

questions.explanation: Same key from both sides is what brings the records together.

questions.question: Name and define the technique that guarantees the reducer sees the user record first.

options.text: Secondary sort: the MapReduce job can be configured so that the reducer always sees the record from the user database first, followed by the activity events in timestamp order. It thus provides two ordering guarantees — the user-database record comes first, and the activity events that follow are in timestamp order
Primary sort, which orders by key only
Total order partitioning, which orders reducers
Combiner ordering, which pre-aggregates on the map side

questions.explanation: Secondary sort orders the values within a key, not just the keys.

questions.question: Walk the reducer's join logic and its output.

options.text: The reducer is called once for every user ID. Thanks to the secondary sort, the first value is expected to be the date-of-birth record from the user database, so the reducer stores the date of birth in a local variable and then iterates over the activity events with the same user ID, outputting pairs of viewed-url and viewer-age-in-years. Subsequent MapReduce jobs could then calculate the distribution of viewer ages for each URL, and cluster by age group
The reducer is called once per activity event and queries the user database
The reducer buffers all records for all users in memory
The reducer emits the raw records unchanged

questions.explanation: Because the reducer processes all of the records for a particular user ID in one go, it only needs to keep one user record in memory at any one time and never needs to make any requests over the network. This algorithm is known as a sort-merge join, since mapper output is sorted by key and the reducers then merge together the sorted lists of records from both sides of the join — a fairly simple, single-threaded piece of code that can churn through records with high throughput and low memory overhead.

questions.question: Explain the chapter's 'mappers send messages to the reducers' metaphor.

options.text: When you think of the key as the destination address to which the value should be delivered, you can see the mappers as sending messages to the reducers. Even though the key is just an arbitrary string — not an actual network address like an IP address and port number — it behaves like an address: all key-value pairs with the same key will be delivered to the same destination, that is, a call to the reducer. A similar idea is behind Pregel: one vertex can 'send a message' to another vertex
The key is literally an IP address and port
The mappers open TCP connections to the reducers directly
The metaphor applies only to Pregel, not to MapReduce

questions.explanation: An address-like key, without being a network address.

questions.question: What two aspects does MapReduce separate, and what extra protection does that buy?

options.text: It separates the physical network communication aspects of the computation — getting the data to the right machine — from the application logic, which is processing the data once you have it. This separation contrasts with the typical use of databases, where a request to fetch data from a database often occurs somewhere deep inside a piece of application code. And since MapReduce handles all network and I/O, it also shields the application code from having to worry about partial failures such as the crash of another node: MapReduce transparently retries failed tasks without affecting the application logic
It separates reads from writes, which buys durability
It separates storage from compute, which buys elasticity
It separates mappers from reducers, which buys nothing extra

questions.explanation: Communication separated from logic, with transparent retries as a bonus.

questions.question: What is the second common use of the 'bring related data together' pattern, and how is it implemented?

options.text: Grouping records by some key, as in the GROUP BY clause in SQL: all records with the same key form a group, and the next step is often to perform some kind of aggregation within each group — counting the number of records in each group as with COUNT(*), adding up the values in one particular field as with SUM(fieldname), or picking the top k records according to some ranking function. The simplest way of implementing such a grouping operation with MapReduce is to set up the mappers so that the key-value pairs they produce use the desired grouping key, then the partitioning and sorting process brings together all the records with the same key in the same reducer. Consequently, grouping and joining look quite similar when implemented on top of MapReduce
Filtering records, implemented in the reducer
Sorting records, implemented by the framework alone
Deduplicating records, implemented by a combiner

questions.explanation: Grouping and joining are structurally the same operation in MapReduce.

questions.question: Define sessionization and its business uses.

options.text: Collating all the activity events for a particular user session, in order to find out the sequence of actions that the user took. If you have multiple web servers handling user requests, the activity events for a particular user are most likely scattered across various different servers' log files — so you can implement sessionization by using a session cookie, user ID or similar identifier as the grouping key and bringing all the activity events for a particular user together in one place, while distributing different users' events across different partitions. The results can be used to work out whether users who were shown a new version of your website are more likely to make a purchase than those shown the old version (A/B testing), or to calculate whether some marketing activity is worthwhile
Splitting one user's events across many servers for load balancing
Counting total page views per day
Deduplicating events by timestamp

questions.explanation: Multiple web servers scattering one user's events is what makes the grouping necessary.

questions.question: What breaks the 'bring all records with the same key to the same place' pattern, and what are its names?

options.text: A very large amount of data related to a single key: for example in a social network most users might be connected to a few hundred people, but a small number of celebrities may have many millions of followers. Such disproportionately active database records are known as linchpin objects or hot keys, and collecting all activity related to a celebrity in a single reducer can lead to significant skew — also known as hot spots — that is, one reducer that must process significantly more records than the others. Since a MapReduce job is only complete when all of its mappers and reducers have completed, any subsequent jobs must wait for the slowest reducer to complete before they can start
Too many distinct keys, known as fan-out
Too few reducers, known as underpartitioning
Unsorted input, known as disorder

questions.explanation: One slow reducer stalls the whole workflow.

questions.question: Describe the skewed join method in Pig.

options.text: It first runs a sampling job to determine which keys are hot. When performing the actual join, the mappers send any records relating to a hot key to one of several reducers, chosen at random — in contrast to conventional MapReduce, which chooses a reducer deterministically based on a hash of the key. For the other input to the join, records relating to the hot key need to be replicated to all reducers handling that key. This technique spreads the work of handling the hot key over several reducers, which allows it to be parallelized better, at the cost of having to replicate the other join input to multiple reducers
It routes all hot-key records to a single dedicated reducer
It drops hot-key records and processes them separately
It hashes hot keys twice to spread them

questions.explanation: Very similar to the technique of using randomization to alleviate hot spots in a partitioned database.

questions.question: Match the three tools to their skew-handling methods.

options.text: Pig's skewed join learns hot keys by running a sampling job first and sends hot-key records to a randomly chosen one of several reducers, replicating the other input. Crunch's sharded join is similar but requires the hot keys to be specified explicitly rather than using a sampling job. Hive's skewed join optimization requires hot keys to be specified explicitly in the table metadata and stores records related to those keys in separate files from the rest, then uses a map-side join for the hot keys
All three use sampling jobs and random reducer assignment
All three require explicit hot-key specification
Pig requires explicit keys; Crunch and Hive use sampling

questions.explanation: Sampling in Pig, explicit specification in Crunch and Hive.

questions.question: For grouping and aggregating by a hot key, what two-stage technique does the chapter prescribe?

options.text: A first MapReduce stage sends records to a random reducer, so that each reducer performs the grouping on a subset of records for the hot key and outputs a more compact aggregated value per key. The second MapReduce job then combines the values from all of the first-stage reducers into a single value per key. The second stage is cheap because its input is only one compact aggregated value per key per first-stage reducer
A single stage with more reducers
A first stage that drops hot keys and a second that reprocesses them
Two stages that both aggregate the full data

questions.explanation: Partial aggregation shrinks the data before the final combine.

questions.question: Why are these called reduce-side joins, and what are the advantage and disadvantage?

options.text: Because they perform the actual join logic in the reducers, with the mappers taking the role of preparing the input data: extracting the key and value from each input record, assigning the key-value pairs to a reducer partition, and sorting by key. The advantage is that you do not need to make any assumptions about the input data — whatever its properties and structure, the mappers can prepare the data to be ready for joining. The downside is that all that sorting, copying to reducers, and merging of reducer inputs can be quite expensive, and depending on the available memory buffers, data may be written to disk several times as it passes through the stages of MapReduce
Because the join happens in the mappers; the advantage is speed
Because the reducers sort; the advantage is that no assumptions are needed and there is no cost
Because HDFS performs the join; the disadvantage is network load

questions.explanation: Generality bought with shuffle cost.

questions.question: What assumption unlocks a map-side join, and what does the job look like?

options.text: If you can make certain assumptions about your input data, it is possible to make joins faster by using a so-called map-side join. This approach uses a cut-down MapReduce job in which there are no reducers and no sorting — instead each mapper simply reads one input file block from the distributed filesystem and writes one output file to the filesystem
It requires more reducers and extra sorting
It requires the input to be unsorted and unpartitioned
It requires a second job to merge results

questions.explanation: No reducers, no sorting — mappers read blocks and write output.

questions.question: State the precondition and algorithm for a broadcast hash join, and explain both halves of the name.

options.text: The precondition: a large dataset is joined with a small dataset that is small enough to be loaded entirely into memory in each of the mappers. The algorithm: each mapper first reads the user database from the distributed filesystem into an in-memory hash table, then scans over the user activity events and simply looks up the user ID for each event in the hash table. There can still be several map tasks — one for each file block of the large input to the join — and each of these mappers loads the small input entirely into memory. The name: 'broadcast' because each mapper for a partition of the large input reads the entirety of the small input, and 'hash' for its use of a hash table
Both inputs must be small; the name refers to broadcasting to reducers
The small input is partitioned; the name refers to a hash partitioner
The large input is loaded into memory; the name is arbitrary

questions.explanation: This join method is supported by Pig under the name replicated join, by Hive as MapJoin, and by Cascading and Crunch; it is also used in data warehouse query engines such as Impala. A footnote notes the description assumes exactly one entry for each key in the hash table, probably true with a user database since a user ID uniquely identifies a user — in general the hash table may need several entries with the same key, and the join operator will output all matches for a key.

questions.question: What is the alternative to an in-memory hash table for the small join input?

options.text: Store the small join input in a read-only index on the local disk. Frequently used parts of this index will remain in the operating system's page cache, so this approach can provide random-access lookups almost as fast as an in-memory hash table, but without actually requiring the dataset to fit in memory
Store it in a remote database and query it per record
Store it in HDFS and read it per record
There is no alternative

questions.explanation: The page cache does the caching for you, lifting the memory constraint.

questions.question: Describe the partitioned hash join for Figure 10-2.

options.text: If the inputs to the map-side join are partitioned in the same way, the hash join approach can be applied to each partition independently: for example you could arrange for the activity events and the user database to each be partitioned based on the last decimal digit of the user ID, so there are 10 partitions on either side. Then mapper 3 first loads all users with an ID ending in 3 into a hash table, and then scans over all the activity events for each user whose ID ends in 3. If the partitioning is done correctly you can be sure that all the records you might want to join are located in the same numbered partition, so it is sufficient for each mapper to only read one partition from each of the input datasets — and each mapper can load a smaller amount of data into its hash table, here about one tenth of the user database
All mappers load the whole user database, as in a broadcast join
Each mapper reads all partitions of both datasets
The partitions must differ between the two sides

questions.explanation: Ten partitions means each hash table is one tenth the size.

questions.question: Under what conditions does a partitioned hash join work, and what does Hive call it?

options.text: It only works if both of the join's inputs have the same number of partitions, with records assigned to partitions according to the same key and the same hash function. This assumption is reasonable if the inputs are generated by prior MapReduce jobs that already perform this grouping. Partitioned hash joins are known as bucketed map joins in Hive
It works if either input is partitioned; Hive calls it a MapJoin
It works if both are sorted but not partitioned; Hive calls it a merge join
It works unconditionally; Hive calls it a skewed join

questions.explanation: Same count, same key, same hash function — all three required.

questions.question: What extra precondition does a map-side merge join need, and why might you run it as a separate job?

options.text: The inputs must be not only partitioned in the same way, but also sorted based on the same key — in which case it does not matter whether the inputs are small enough to fit in memory, because a mapper can perform the same merging operation that would normally be done by a reducer: reading both input files incrementally, in order of ascending key, and matching records with the same key. If a map-side merge join is possible it probably means that prior MapReduce jobs brought the input datasets into this partitioned and sorted form in the first place — in principle this join could have been performed in the reduce stage of the prior job, but it may still be appropriate to perform the merge join in a separate map-only job, for example if the partitioned and sorted datasets are also needed for other purposes besides this particular join
The inputs must be small enough to fit in memory
The inputs must be unsorted, since the mapper sorts them
The inputs must be in the same file

questions.explanation: No hash table is needed at all — it's a streaming merge.

questions.question: How does the choice of join affect the output layout, and where does the needed metadata live?

options.text: The output of a reduce-side join is partitioned and sorted by the join key, whereas the output of a map-side join is partitioned and sorted in the same way as the large input, since one map task is started for each file block of the join's large input regardless of whether a partitioned or broadcast join is used. To optimize join strategies it is not sufficient to just know the encoding format and the name of the directory in which the data is stored — you must also know the number of partitions and the keys by which the data is partitioned and sorted. In the Hadoop ecosystem this kind of metadata about the partitioning of datasets is often maintained in HCatalog and the Hive metastore
Both joins produce output sorted by the join key; metadata lives in HDFS block headers
Neither join affects output layout; metadata is unnecessary
Map-side joins produce unsorted output; metadata lives in ZooKeeper

questions.explanation: The output layout is inherited from the side that drives the mappers.

questions.question: Where does batch processing sit relative to OLTP and analytics?

options.text: OLTP queries generally look up a small number of records by key using indexes, in order to present them to a user; analytic queries scan over a large number of records, performing groupings and aggregations, with output often in the form of a report — such as a chart or a table of top 10 items — read by an analyst or a manager who needs to make business decisions. Batch processing is neither transaction processing nor analytics: it is closer to analytics in that it scans over large portions of an input dataset, but it is not the same as a SQL query used for analytic purposes, since the output of a batch process is often not a report but some other kind of structure
Batch processing is a form of transaction processing
Batch processing is identical to analytics
Batch processing always produces reports

questions.explanation: Analytics-shaped access, but a different kind of output.

questions.question: What was MapReduce originally built for at Google, and how many jobs did it take?

options.text: Google's original use of MapReduce was to build indexes for its search engine, implemented as a workflow of 5 to 10 MapReduce jobs. Although Google later moved away from using MapReduce for this purpose, it helps to understand MapReduce if you look at it through the lens of building a search index — and even today, Hadoop MapReduce remains a good way of building indexes for Lucene/Solr
Building the web crawl, in 50 to 100 jobs
Computing PageRank, in a single job
Serving search queries, in 5 to 10 jobs

questions.explanation: Note the contrast in scale: 5 to 10 jobs for search indexing versus 50 to 100 for recommendation systems.

questions.question: How does a batch process build a search index, and why are the outputs immutable?

options.text: If you need to perform a full-text search over a fixed set of documents, a batch process is a very effective way of building the indexes: the mappers partition the set of documents as needed, each reducer builds the index for its partition, and the index files are written to the distributed filesystem. Since querying such an index by keyword is a read-only operation, these index files are immutable once they have been created. Building document-partitioned indexes parallelizes very well
The mappers build the index and the reducers query it; outputs are mutable
A single reducer builds a global index; outputs are mutable
Indexes are built at query time, so there are no output files

questions.explanation: A Lucene-style full-text index is a file — the term dictionary — in which you can efficiently look up a particular keyword and find the list of all the document IDs containing that keyword, the postings list. A real index needs various additional data to rank search results by relevance, correct misspellings and resolve synonyms.

questions.question: Contrast the two ways to keep an index up to date.

options.text: Full rebuild: periodically rerun the entire indexing workflow for the entire set of documents and replace the previous index files wholesale with the new ones when it is done. This can be computationally expensive if only a small number of documents have changed, but it has the advantage that the indexing process is very easy to reason about — documents in, indexes out. Incremental: it is also possible to build indexes incrementally; as discussed in Chapter 3, if you want to add, remove or update documents in an index, Lucene writes out new segment files and asynchronously merges and compacts segment files in the background, with more on such incremental processing in Chapter 11
Full rebuild is cheap and incremental is expensive
Only incremental indexing is possible
Only full rebuilds are possible

questions.explanation: Simplicity versus efficiency, with segment merging as the incremental mechanism.

questions.question: What machine learning outputs does the chapter name, and what problem do they create?

options.text: Classifiers such as spam filters, anomaly detection and image recognition, and recommendation systems for people you may know, products you may be interested in, or related searches. The output of these batch jobs is often some kind of database — for example a database that can be queried by user ID to obtain suggested friends, or queried by product ID to get a list of related products. These databases need to be queried from the web application that handles user requests, which is usually separate from the Hadoop infrastructure. So how does the output from the batch process get back into a database where the web application can query it?
Only classifiers; the output is always a report
Only recommendation systems; the output stays in HDFS
Neither; machine learning is out of scope

questions.explanation: Two families, both producing databases that must be served from outside Hadoop.

questions.question: Why is writing to the database from inside a mapper or reducer a bad idea? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Making a network request for every single record is orders of magnitude slower than the normal throughput of a batch task, and even if the client library supports batching, performance is likely to be poor

MapReduce jobs often run many tasks in parallel, so if all the mappers or reducers concurrently write to the same output database, that database can easily be overwhelmed — which can in turn cause operational problems in other parts of the system

Writing to an external system from inside a job produces externally visible side effects that cannot be hidden, so you have to worry about the results from partially completed jobs being visible to other systems, especially given Hadoop task attempts and speculative execution
Databases cannot accept writes from more than one client

questions.explanation: The chapter also notes in passing that this only works at all if firewall rules allow direct access from your Hadoop environment to your production databases.

questions.question: State MapReduce's all-or-nothing guarantee.

options.text: MapReduce provides a clean all-or-nothing guarantee for job output: if a job succeeds, the result is the output of running every task exactly once, even if some tasks failed and had to be retried along the way; and if the entire job fails, no output is produced. Because inputs are immutable and outputs from failed tasks are discarded, tasks can be retried safely — and if several tasks for a partition succeed, only one of them actually makes its output visible
Partial output is visible during execution and cleaned up afterward
Every task's output is visible, including retries
The guarantee applies only to reducers, not mappers

questions.explanation: Exactly-once effect from at-least-once execution, achieved by discarding losers.

questions.question: What is the right way to ship batch output into a serving database?

options.text: Build a brand-new database inside the batch job and write it as files to the job's output directory in the distributed filesystem — immutable once written, and able to be loaded in bulk into servers that handle read-only queries. Various key-value stores support building database files in MapReduce jobs, including Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB and HBase bulk loading. Building these database files is a good use of MapReduce: using a mapper to extract a key and then sorting by that key is already a lot of the work required to build an index, and since most of these databases are read-only the data structures are quite simple — for example they do not require a write-ahead log
Write directly to the production database from the reducer, in batches
Export to CSV and import manually
Stream the output through a message queue into the database

questions.explanation: When loading data into Voldemort, the server continues serving requests to the old data files while the new data files are copied from the distributed filesystem to the server's local disk; once copying is complete, the server atomically switches over to querying the new files. If anything goes wrong it can easily switch back to the old files again, since they are still there and immutable.

questions.question: State the Unix dataflow discipline the chapter restates, and its maintainability benefits. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A program reads its input and writes its output; in the process, the input is left unchanged, any previous output is completely replaced with the new output, and there are no other side effects. This means you can rerun a command as often as you like, tweaking or debugging it, without messing up the state of your system

If you introduce a bug into the code and the output is wrong or corrupted, you can simply roll back to a previous version of the code and rerun the job, and the output will be correct again — or even more simply, keep the old output in a different directory and switch back to it. Databases with read-write transactions do not have this property: if you deploy buggy code that writes bad data to the database, rolling back the code will do nothing to fix the data. This ability to recover from buggy code has been called human fault tolerance

As a consequence of this ease of rolling back, feature development can proceed more quickly than in an environment where mistakes could mean irreversible damage — this principle of minimizing irreversibility is beneficial for Agile software development

If a map or reduce task fails, the MapReduce framework automatically reschedules it and runs it again on the same input; if the failure is due to a bug the code will keep crashing and eventually cause the job to fail after a few attempts, but if the failure is transient the fault is tolerated. This automatic retry is only safe because inputs are immutable and outputs from failed tasks are discarded
