questions.explanation: Also on the list: the same set of files can be used as input for various different jobs, including monitoring jobs that calculate metrics and evaluate whether a job's output has the expected characteristics — for example by comparing it to the output from the previous run and measuring discrepancies.

questions.question: What difference between Unix and Hadoop does the chapter identify, and how does Hadoop resolve it?

options.text: Like Unix tools, MapReduce jobs separate logic from wiring — configuring input and output directories — which provides a separation of concerns and enables potential reuse of code: one team can focus on implementing a job that does one thing well, while other teams can decide where and when to run that job. However, in the Unix world the uniform interface that allows one program to be composed with another is just untyped text files, whereas in the Hadoop world some of those rough edges are removed by implementing more structured file formats such as Avro and Parquet — so at least a level of value-based schema conversion is provided and low-value syntactic conversions are eliminated
Hadoop uses text files and Unix uses structured formats
There is no difference; both use untyped text
Hadoop eliminates the need for any interface

questions.explanation: Avro and Parquet remove the parsing tax that {print $7} represents.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say the MapReduce paper was 'not at all new'?

options.text: Because all of the processing and parallel join algorithms it discusses had already been implemented in so-called massively parallel processing (MPP) databases more than a decade previously — the Gamma database machine, Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL were pioneers in this area. The biggest difference is that MPP databases focus on parallel execution of analytic SQL queries on a cluster of machines, while the combination of MapReduce and a distributed filesystem provides something much more like a general-purpose operating system that can run arbitrary programs
Because MapReduce was copied from Hadoop
Because MapReduce was described in the 1978 Unix paper
Because MPP databases postdate MapReduce

questions.explanation: Generality is the difference, not the algorithms.

questions.question: What does a database require of your data that a distributed filesystem does not?

options.text: Databases require you to structure data according to a particular model — relational or documents — whereas files in a distributed filesystem are just byte sequences, which can be written using any data model and encoding. They might be collections of database records, but they can equally well be text, images, videos, sensor readings, sparse matrices, feature vectors, genome sequences or any other kind of data
Databases require sorted input; filesystems do not
Databases require immutable data; filesystems allow mutation
There is no difference in requirements

questions.explanation: Hadoop opened up the possibility of indiscriminately dumping data into HDFS and only later figuring out how to process it further, whereas MPP databases typically require careful up-front modeling of the data and query patterns before importing the data into the database's proprietary storage format. From a purist's point of view careful modeling and import is desirable because users have better-quality data to work with — but in practice, simply making data available quickly, even in a quirky, difficult-to-use, raw format, is often more valuable than trying to decide on the ideal data model up front.

questions.question: Which named ideas does the chapter use to describe raw-first data collection? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data lake or enterprise data hub: bringing data from various parts of a large organization together in one place is valuable, because it enables joins across datasets that were previously disparate — and the careful schema design required by an MPP database slows down that centralized data collection, so collecting data in its raw form and worrying about schema design later speeds it up

Schema-on-read: indiscriminate data dumping shifts the burden of interpreting the data from the producer to the consumer, which can be an advantage if the producer and consumers are different teams with different priorities — and there may not even be one ideal data model, but rather different views onto the data that are suitable for different purposes
The sushi principle: 'raw data is better'
The waterfall principle: 'model first, load later'

questions.explanation: Three names for the same raw-first discipline.

questions.question: Describe the ETL pattern the chapter says Hadoop is often used for.

options.text: Data from transaction processing systems is dumped into the distributed filesystem in some raw form, and then MapReduce jobs are written to clean up that data, transform it into a relational form, and import it into an MPP data warehouse for analytic purposes. Data modeling still happens, but it is in a separate step, decoupled from the data collection — and this decoupling is possible because a distributed filesystem supports data encoded in any format
Hadoop replaces the warehouse entirely, so no ETL is needed
The warehouse performs the ETL and Hadoop stores the results
ETL is performed by the transaction processing systems themselves

questions.explanation: So Hadoop and the MPP warehouse are complements, not only competitors.

questions.question: What does 'monolithic' buy an MPP database?

options.text: MPP databases are monolithic, tightly integrated pieces of software that take care of storage layout on disk, query planning, scheduling and execution. Since these components can all be tuned and optimized for the specific needs of the database, the system as a whole can achieve very good performance on the types of queries for which it is designed. Moreover the SQL query language allows expressive queries and elegant semantics without the need to write code, making it accessible to graphical tools used by business analysts, such as Tableau
Monolithic design buys flexibility at the cost of performance
Monolithic design buys nothing; it is purely a liability
Monolithic design buys arbitrary code execution

questions.explanation: Tight integration buys tuned performance and analyst-accessible SQL.

questions.question: Which workloads need a more general model than SQL, and why code rather than queries?

options.text: Not all kinds of processing can be sensibly expressed as SQL queries: machine learning and recommendation systems, full-text search indexes with relevance ranking models, and image analysis all need a more general model of data processing. These kinds of processing are often very specific to a particular application — for example feature engineering for machine learning, natural language models for machine translation, or risk estimation functions for fraud prediction — and so they inevitably require writing code, not just queries. MapReduce gave engineers the ability to easily run their own code over large datasets; and if you have HDFS and MapReduce you can build a SQL query execution engine on top of it, which is indeed what the Hive project did
Only reporting workloads need code; everything else fits SQL
SQL can express all these workloads without extension
These workloads require specialized hardware, not code

questions.explanation: Application-specific logic is what resists a declarative query language.

questions.question: Why were two processing models not enough?

options.text: Because MapReduce was too limiting and performed too badly for some types of processing, so various other processing models were developed on top of Hadoop. Having two processing models, SQL and MapReduce, was not enough: even more different models were needed. And due to the openness of the Hadoop platform it was feasible to implement a whole range of approaches, which would not have been possible within the confines of a monolithic MPP database
Because SQL was too slow and MapReduce too fast
Because two models are always sufficient; the chapter argues against more
Because MPP databases already offered every model

questions.explanation: Platform openness is what let the ecosystem proliferate.

questions.question: What is the single shared-use cluster argument, and which two Hadoop-ecosystem systems illustrate it?

options.text: Crucially, those various processing models can all be run on a single shared-use cluster of machines, all accessing the same files on the distributed filesystem — so in the Hadoop approach there is no need to import the data into several different specialized systems for different kinds of processing: the system is flexible enough to support a diverse set of workloads within the same cluster. Not having to move data around makes it a lot easier to derive value from the data, and a lot easier to experiment with new processing models. Random-access OLTP databases such as HBase and MPP-style analytic databases such as Impala illustrate this: neither HBase nor Impala uses MapReduce, but both use HDFS for storage, so very different approaches to accessing and processing data can coexist and be integrated in the same system
Each processing model requires its own cluster; HBase and Impala have separate storage
Only MapReduce-based systems can share a cluster
The shared cluster argument applies only to storage, not processing

questions.explanation: Shared HDFS, divergent engines.

questions.question: What two further design differences does the chapter highlight between MPP databases and MapReduce?

options.text: The handling of faults and the use of memory and disk. Batch processes are less sensitive to faults than online systems, because they do not immediately affect users if they fail and they can always be run again. So if a node crashes while a query is executing, most MPP databases abort the entire query and either let the user resubmit the query or automatically run it again, whereas MapReduce can tolerate the failure of a map or reduce task without it affecting the job as a whole by retrying work at the granularity of an individual task. MPP databases also prefer to keep as much data as possible in memory — for example using hash joins — to avoid the cost of reading from disk, whereas MapReduce is very eager to write data to disk, partly for fault tolerance and partly on the assumption that the dataset will be too big to fit in memory anyway
The choice of query language and the storage format
The network topology and the scheduling policy
The isolation level and the replication factor

questions.explanation: MPP queries normally run for a few seconds or a few minutes at most, so the cost of retrying the entire query is not too great — whereas MapReduce jobs process so much data and run for so long that they are likely to experience at least one task failure along the way.

questions.question: Describe the environment MapReduce was designed for.

options.text: Google has mixed-use datacenters, in which online production services and offline batch jobs run on the same machines. Every task has a resource allocation — CPU cores, RAM, disk space and so on — that is enforced using containers, and every task also has a priority: if a higher-priority task needs more resources, lower-priority tasks on the same machine can be terminated, that is preempted, in order to free up resources. Priority also determines pricing of the computing resources: teams must pay for the resources they use, and higher-priority processes cost more. This architecture allows non-production computing resources to be overcommitted, because the system knows that it can reclaim them if necessary — so batch jobs effectively pick up the scraps under the table
Dedicated batch-only clusters with no priority system
Rented cloud VMs with no preemption
Supercomputers with checkpointing

questions.explanation: The chapter asks how realistic the fault assumptions are: in most clusters machine failures do occur but are not very frequent — probably rare enough that most jobs will not experience a machine failure — so is it really worth incurring significant overheads for the sake of fault tolerance? The answer is that preemption, not hardware failure, is the dominant cause of termination.

questions.question: Give Google's preemption figures and the 100-task claim.

options.text: At Google, a MapReduce task that runs for an hour has an approximately 5% risk of being terminated to make space for a higher-priority process — a rate more than an order of magnitude higher than the rate of failures due to hardware issues, machine reboot, or other reasons. At this rate, if a job has 100 tasks that each run for 10 minutes, there is a risk greater than 50% that at least one task will be terminated before it is finished
A 50% risk per hour, giving near-certain termination for 100 tasks
A 0.5% risk per hour, giving a 5% risk for 100 tasks
A 5% risk per day, giving a 50% risk for 1,000 tasks

questions.explanation: A 10-minute task is one sixth of an hour, giving roughly a 0.85% chance of being killed per task, so the chance that at least one of 100 survives-free is about 0.9915 to the hundredth power, leaving roughly a 57% chance of at least one kill — consistent with the chapter's 'greater than 50%'.

questions.question: What is the real reason MapReduce tolerates frequent termination, and who else preempts?

options.text: This is why MapReduce is designed to tolerate frequent unexpected task termination: it's not because the hardware is particularly unreliable, it's because the freedom to arbitrarily terminate processes enables better resource utilization in a computing cluster. Among open source cluster schedulers, preemption is less widely used: YARN's CapacityScheduler supports preemption for balancing the resource allocation of different queues, but general priority preemption is not supported in YARN, Mesos or Kubernetes at the time of writing. In an environment where tasks are not so often terminated, the design decisions of MapReduce make less sense
Because commodity hardware fails constantly; all open source schedulers preempt
Because networks are unreliable; only Mesos preempts
Because disks wear out; Kubernetes preempts by default

questions.explanation: Utilization, not unreliability, is the design driver.

questions.question: Why did the chapter spend so long on MapReduce, and what distinction does it draw about 'simple'?

options.text: MapReduce became very popular and received a lot of hype in the late 2000s, but it is just one among many possible programming models for distributed systems — depending on the volume of data, the structure of the data, and the type of processing being done with it, other tools may be more appropriate. The chapter dwells on it because it is a useful learning tool, being a fairly clear and simple abstraction on top of a distributed filesystem: simple in the sense of being able to understand what it is doing, not in the sense of being easy to use. Quite the opposite — implementing a complex processing job using the raw MapReduce APIs is actually quite hard and laborious; for instance you would need to implement any join algorithms from scratch
Because MapReduce is easy to use and remains the fastest option
Because MapReduce is the only available model
Because MapReduce is simple in both senses of the word

questions.explanation: Understandable, not easy — a distinction worth keeping straight.

questions.question: What did the higher-level programming models fix, and what could they not fix?

options.text: Higher-level programming models such as Pig, Hive, Cascading and Crunch were created as abstractions on top of MapReduce; they are fairly easy to learn, and their higher-level constructs make many common batch processing tasks significantly easier to implement. But they could not fix problems with the MapReduce execution model itself, which are not fixed by adding another level of abstraction and which manifest themselves as poor performance for some kinds of processing
They fixed the execution model and left the API unchanged
They fixed both the API and the execution model
They fixed nothing

questions.explanation: Abstraction cannot fix an execution model. On the one hand MapReduce is very robust: you can use it to process almost arbitrarily large quantities of data on an unreliable multi-tenant system with frequent task terminations, and it will still get the job done, albeit slowly. On the other hand, other tools are sometimes orders of magnitude faster for some kinds of processing.

questions.question: Define materialization and contrast it with what Unix pipes do.

options.text: The process of writing out intermediate state to files is called materialization — meaning to eagerly compute the result of some operation and write it out, rather than computing it on demand when requested, as with materialized views. By contrast, Unix pipes do not fully materialize the intermediate state, but instead stream the output to the input incrementally, using only a small in-memory buffer
Materialization means computing on demand; pipes materialize fully
Both materialize fully; the difference is the storage medium
Neither materializes; both stream

questions.explanation: A dataset is intermediate state rather than a published dataset when the output of one job is only ever used as input to one other job maintained by the same team — and in a workflow of 50 or 100 MapReduce jobs there is a lot of such intermediate state. By contrast, if the output from the first job is a dataset you want to publish widely within your organization, other teams can refer to it by name and reuse it as input to several different jobs, and publishing data to a well-known location in the distributed filesystem allows loose coupling so that jobs don't need to know who is producing their input or consuming their output.

questions.question: What are the downsides of MapReduce's full materialization? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: No overlap between stages: a MapReduce job can only start when all tasks in the preceding jobs that generate its inputs have completed, whereas processes connected by a Unix pipe are started at the same time with output being consumed as soon as it is produced. Skew or varying load on different machines means a job often has a few straggler tasks that take much longer than the others, and having to wait for all of the preceding job's tasks slows down the execution of the workflow as a whole

Redundant mappers: mappers are often redundant, just reading back the same file that was just written by a reducer and preparing it for the next stage of partitioning and sorting — in many cases the mapper code could be part of the previous reducer, so if the reducer output was partitioned and sorted in the same way as mapper output, then reducers could be chained together directly without interleaving with mapper stages
Over-replication of temporary data: storing intermediate state in a distributed filesystem means those files are replicated across several nodes, which is often overkill for such temporary data
Loss of fault tolerance, since materialized files cannot be re-read

questions.explanation: Materialized files are precisely what makes MapReduce's fault tolerance easy — the trade-off runs the other way.

questions.question: Name the three best-known dataflow engines and what they share.

options.text: Spark, Tez and Flink. They have one thing in common: they handle an entire workflow as one job, rather than breaking it up into independent subjobs. Since they explicitly model the flow of data through several processing stages, these systems are known as dataflow engines. Like MapReduce they work by repeatedly calling a user-defined function to process one record at a time on a single thread, and they parallelize work by partitioning inputs and copying the output of one function over the network to become the input to another function
Hive, Pig and Cascading, which share a declarative API
HBase, Impala and Drill, which share HDFS storage
Oozie, Azkaban and Airflow, which share a scheduler

questions.explanation: This style of processing engine is based on research systems like Dryad and Nephele.

questions.question: Define operator, and give the three ways a dataflow engine can wire one operator's output to another's input. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Unlike in MapReduce, these functions need not take the strict roles of alternating map and reduce, but instead can be assembled in more flexible ways — these functions are called operators
One option is to repartition and sort records by key, like the shuffle stage of MapReduce, which enables sort-merge joins and grouping in the same way as in MapReduce

Another option is to take several inputs and partition them in the same way but skip the sorting — saving effort on partitioned hash joins, where the partitioning of records is important but the order is irrelevant because building the hash table randomizes the order anyway
For broadcast hash joins, the same output from one operator can be sent to all partitions of the join operator

questions.explanation: Sorting becomes opt-in per connection rather than unconditional.

questions.question: Which advantages do dataflow engines have over MapReduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Expensive work such as sorting need only be performed in places where it is actually required, rather than always happening by default between every map and reduce stage; and there are no unnecessary map tasks, since the work done by a mapper can often be incorporated into the preceding reduce operator because a mapper does not change the partitioning of a dataset

Because all joins and data dependencies in a workflow are explicitly declared, the scheduler has an overview of what data is required where, so it can make locality optimizations — for example placing the task that consumes some data on the same machine as the task that produces it, so the data can be exchanged through a shared memory buffer rather than having to copy it over the network

It is usually sufficient for intermediate state between operators to be kept in memory or written to local disk, which requires less I/O than writing it to HDFS where it must be replicated to several machines and written to disk on each replica — and MapReduce already uses this optimization for mapper output, but dataflow engines generalize the idea to all intermediate state

Operators can start executing as soon as their input is ready, with no need to wait for the entire preceding stage to finish; and existing JVM processes can be reused to run new operators, reducing startup overheads compared to MapReduce, which launches a new JVM for each task

questions.explanation: Six advantages. You can use dataflow engines to implement the same computations as MapReduce workflows and they usually execute significantly faster — and since operators are a generalization of map and reduce, the same processing code can run on either execution engine: workflows implemented in Pig, Hive or Cascading can be switched from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with a simple configuration change, without modifying code.

questions.question: Contrast Tez with Spark and Flink as pieces of software.

options.text: Tez is a fairly thin library that relies on the YARN shuffle service for the actual copying of data between nodes, whereas Spark and Flink are big frameworks that include their own network communication layer, scheduler and user-facing APIs
Tez is the largest framework; Spark and Flink are thin libraries
All three are thin libraries over YARN
All three ship their own scheduler and network layer

questions.explanation: Tez borrows; Spark and Flink ship their own.

questions.question: How do Spark, Flink and Tez tolerate faults without materializing to HDFS?

options.text: An advantage of fully materializing intermediate state to a distributed filesystem is that it is durable, which makes fault tolerance fairly easy in MapReduce: if a task fails it can just be restarted on another machine and read the same input again from the filesystem. Spark, Flink and Tez avoid writing intermediate state to HDFS, so they take a different approach: if a machine fails and the intermediate state on that machine is lost, it is recomputed from other data that is still available — a prior intermediary stage if possible, or otherwise the original input data, which is normally on HDFS. To enable this recomputation, the framework must keep track of how a given piece of data was computed: which input partitions it used, and which operators were applied to it. Spark uses the resilient distributed dataset (RDD) abstraction for tracking the ancestry of data, while Flink checkpoints operator state, allowing it to resume running an operator that ran into a fault during its execution
They replicate intermediate state to three machines, like HDFS
They restart the whole job on any failure
They do not tolerate faults

questions.explanation: Lineage in Spark, operator checkpoints in Flink.

questions.question: Why does determinism matter when recomputing, and how does nondeterminism creep in? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The question matters if some of the lost data has already been sent to downstream operators: if the operator is restarted and the recomputed data is not the same as the original lost data, it becomes very hard for downstream operators to resolve the contradictions between the old and new data — so the remedy for nondeterministic operators is normally to kill the downstream operators as well and run them again on the new data. In order to avoid such cascading faults, it is better to make operators deterministic
Many programming languages do not guarantee any particular order when iterating over elements of a hash table
Many probabilistic and statistical algorithms explicitly rely on using random numbers

Any use of the system clock or external data sources is nondeterministic. Such causes of nondeterminism need to be removed in order to reliably recover from faults, for example by generating pseudorandom numbers using a fixed seed

questions.explanation: Recovering by recomputing data is not always the right answer: if the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or if the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is probably cheaper to materialize the intermediate data to files than to recompute it.

questions.question: Restate the Unix analogy for materialization, and name the one operator that cannot be pipelined.

options.text: MapReduce is like writing the output of each command to a temporary file, whereas dataflow engines look much more like Unix pipes. Flink especially is built around the idea of pipelined execution: incrementally passing the output of an operator to other operators, and not waiting for the input to be complete before starting to process it. A sorting operation inevitably needs to consume its entire input before it can produce any output, because it's possible that the very last input record is the one with the lowest key and thus needs to be the very first output record — so any operator that requires sorting will need to accumulate state, at least temporarily. But many other parts of a workflow can be executed in a pipelined manner
Filtering is the blocking operator; sorting can be pipelined
Joining is the blocking operator; sorting can be pipelined
No operator blocks in a dataflow engine

questions.explanation: Sorting is inherently blocking. When the job completes its output needs to go somewhere durable so that users can find it and use it — most likely written to the distributed filesystem again. So with a dataflow engine, materialized datasets on HDFS are still usually the inputs and the final outputs of a job: like with MapReduce the inputs are immutable and the output is completely replaced, and the improvement is that you save writing all the intermediate state to the filesystem. Pipes in the middle, files at the edges.

questions.question: How does batch graph processing differ from Chapter 2's graph use, and what does PageRank compute?

options.text: Chapter 2 discussed using graphs for modeling data and graph query languages to traverse edges and vertices, focused around OLTP-style use: quickly executing queries to find a small number of vertices matching certain criteria. In a batch processing context the goal is to perform some kind of offline processing or analysis on an entire graph — a need that often arises in machine learning applications such as recommendation engines, or in ranking systems. One of the most famous graph analysis algorithms is PageRank, which tries to estimate the popularity of a web page based on what other web pages link to it, and is used as part of the formula that determines the order in which web search engines present their results
Batch graph processing finds single vertices quickly; Chapter 2 analyzed whole graphs
They are the same use case at different scales
PageRank ranks users by activity

questions.explanation: Whole-graph analysis rather than targeted traversal.

questions.question: The chapter interrupts itself with a boxed warning about DAGs. What does it say?

options.text: Dataflow engines like Spark, Flink and Tez typically arrange the operators in a job as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). This is not the same as graph processing: in dataflow engines the flow of data from one operator to another is structured as a graph, while the data itself typically consists of relational-style tuples; in graph processing, the data itself has the form of a graph. Another unfortunate naming confusion
DAGs and graph processing are the same thing
Graph processing requires a cyclic operator graph
The box warns that DAGs cannot express graph algorithms

questions.explanation: Graph-shaped topology versus graph-shaped data.

questions.question: How are many graph algorithms expressed, and what is the chapter's worked example?

options.text: Many graph algorithms are expressed by traversing one edge at a time, joining one vertex with an adjacent vertex in order to propagate some information, and repeating until some condition is met — for example until there are no more edges to follow, or until some metric converges. The example from Figure 2-6 is making a list of all the locations in North America contained in a database by repeatedly following edges indicating which location is within which other location — an algorithm known as a transitive closure
By a single pass over all edges; the example is PageRank
By sorting vertices by degree; the example is clustering
By recursive SQL; the example is a join

questions.explanation: Repeat-until-converged is the shape, and transitive closure is the name of the example.

questions.question: Why does 'repeating until done' break plain MapReduce, and what is the workaround?

options.text: It is possible to store a graph in a distributed filesystem, in files containing lists of vertices and edges, but this idea of 'repeating until done' cannot be expressed in plain MapReduce since it only performs a single pass over the data. The algorithm thus has to be implemented in an iterative style: an external scheduler runs a batch process to calculate one step of the algorithm; when the batch process completes the scheduler checks whether it has finished, based on the completion condition — for example there are no more edges to follow, or the change compared to the last iteration is below some threshold; and if it has not yet finished, the scheduler goes back to step 1 and runs another round
MapReduce supports iteration natively, so no workaround is needed
The reducer loops internally until convergence
The graph must be processed on a single machine

questions.explanation: This works, but implementing it with MapReduce is often very inefficient, because MapReduce does not account for the iterative nature of the algorithm: it will always read the entire input dataset and produce a completely new output dataset, even if only a small part of the graph has changed compared to the last iteration.

questions.question: Name the model that fixes this, its alternative name, and its implementations.

options.text: The bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) model of computation, which has become popular for batch processing graphs. It is implemented in Apache Giraph, Spark's GraphX API and Flink's Gelly API, and is also known as the Pregel model, as Google's Pregel paper popularized this approach for processing graphs
The MapReduce iteration model, implemented in Oozie
The dataflow model, implemented in Spark and Flink only
The actor model, implemented in Akka

questions.explanation: BSP and Pregel are two names for the same model.

questions.question: Describe Pregel's message-passing model and its crucial difference from MapReduce.

options.text: Recall that in MapReduce, mappers conceptually 'send a message' to a particular call of the reducer because the framework collects together all the mapper outputs with the same key. A similar idea is behind Pregel: one vertex can 'send a message' to another vertex, and typically those messages are sent along the edges in a graph. In each iteration a function is called for each vertex, passing it all the messages that were sent to it — much like a call to the reducer. The difference from MapReduce is that in the Pregel model a vertex remembers its state in memory from one iteration to the next, so the function only needs to process new incoming messages, and if no messages are being sent in some part of the graph, no work needs to be done
Pregel is stateless like MapReduce, but sends messages along edges
Pregel processes all vertices every iteration regardless of activity
Pregel eliminates message passing in favour of shared memory

questions.explanation: Persistent vertex state means work is proportional to activity, not graph size.

questions.question: How does Pregel differ from the actor model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Vertex state and messages between vertices are fault-tolerant and durable, and communication is guaranteed
Communication proceeds in fixed rounds: at every iteration the framework delivers all messages sent in the previous iteration, whereas actors normally have no such timing guarantee
Vertices cannot send messages at all, unlike actors
Pregel has no state, unlike actors

questions.explanation: Durability and round-based delivery are the two differences. The fact that vertices can only communicate by message passing, not by querying each other directly, helps improve the performance of Pregel jobs, since messages can be batched and there is less waiting for communication. The only waiting is between iterations: since the model guarantees that all messages sent in one iteration are delivered in the next, the prior iteration must completely finish and all of its messages must be copied over the network before the next one can start. Even though the underlying network may drop, duplicate or arbitrarily delay messages, Pregel implementations guarantee that messages are processed exactly once at their destination vertex in the following iteration.

questions.question: How does Pregel achieve fault tolerance?

options.text: By periodically checkpointing the state of all vertices at the end of an iteration — that is, writing their full state to durable storage. If a node fails and its in-memory state is lost, the simplest solution is to roll back the entire graph computation to the last checkpoint and restart. If the algorithm is deterministic and messages are logged, it is also possible to selectively recover only the partition that was lost, as with dataflow engines
By replicating all vertex state synchronously to three machines
By recomputing from the original input on every failure with no checkpoints
It does not tolerate faults

questions.explanation: Checkpoints for the simple case, determinism plus message logs for selective recovery.

questions.question: What does a vertex know about its physical placement, and how are graphs partitioned in practice?

options.text: A vertex does not need to know on which physical machine it is executing; when it sends messages to other vertices it simply sends them to a vertex ID. It is up to the framework to partition the graph — to decide which vertex runs on which machine, and how to route messages over the network so that they end up in the right place. Because the programming model deals with just one vertex at a time, sometimes called 'thinking like a vertex', the framework may partition the graph in arbitrary ways. Ideally it would be partitioned such that vertices are colocated on the same machine if they need to communicate a lot — however finding such an optimized partitioning is hard, so in practice the graph is often simply partitioned by an arbitrarily assigned vertex ID, making no attempt to group related vertices together
A vertex must specify the target machine when sending messages
The framework always finds the optimal partitioning
Graphs cannot be partitioned in Pregel

questions.explanation: Thinking like a vertex, with arbitrary partitioning in practice.

questions.question: Given the communication overhead, when should you not use a distributed graph algorithm?

options.text: Graph algorithms often have a lot of cross-machine communication overhead, and the intermediate state — messages sent between nodes — is often bigger than the original graph, so sending messages over the network can significantly slow things down. If your graph can fit in memory on a single computer, it's quite likely that a single-machine, maybe even single-threaded, algorithm will outperform a distributed batch process. Even if the graph is bigger than memory but can fit on the disks of a single computer, single-machine processing using a framework such as GraphChi is a viable option. If the graph is too big to fit on a single machine, a distributed approach such as Pregel is unavoidable — and efficiently parallelizing graph algorithms is an area of ongoing research
Always use a distributed algorithm; single machines are never competitive
Never use a distributed algorithm; graphs always fit on one machine
Use distributed algorithms only for graphs smaller than memory

questions.explanation: The same lesson as the single-machine awk/sort pipeline beating a Hadoop cluster.

questions.question: What scale figures does the chapter use to declare the physical problem solved, and where did attention turn?

options.text: The infrastructure has become robust enough to store and process many petabytes of data on clusters of over 10,000 machines. As the problem of physically operating batch processes at such scale has been considered more or less solved, attention has turned to other areas: improving the programming model, improving the efficiency of processing, and broadening the set of problems that these technologies can solve
Clusters of 100 machines and terabytes; attention turned to hardware
Clusters of 1,000 machines; attention turned to security
Clusters of 100,000 machines; attention turned to networking

questions.explanation: Compare against the earlier figure: HDFS deployments on tens of thousands of machines with hundreds of petabytes.

questions.question: Why did the high-level languages win twice?

options.text: Higher-level languages and APIs such as Hive, Pig, Cascading and Crunch became popular because programming MapReduce jobs by hand is quite laborious. As Tez emerged, these high-level languages had the additional benefit of being able to move to the new dataflow execution engine without the need to rewrite job code. Spark and Flink also include their own high-level dataflow APIs, often taking inspiration from FlumeJava
Because they were faster than raw MapReduce and required no rewrite for SQL
Because they supported streaming from the start
Because they eliminated the need for a cluster

questions.explanation: Less code first, then engine portability for free. These dataflow APIs generally use relational-style building blocks to express a computation: joining datasets on the value of some field, grouping tuples by key, filtering by some condition, and aggregating tuples by counting, summing or other functions — implemented internally using the various join and grouping algorithms discussed in the chapter.

questions.question: Beyond less code, what advantage do high-level interfaces bring?

options.text: They allow interactive use, in which you write analysis code incrementally in a shell and run it frequently to observe what it is doing. This style of development is very helpful when exploring a dataset and experimenting with approaches for processing it — and it is also reminiscent of the Unix philosophy, specifically its third property of transparency and experimentation. Moreover, these high-level interfaces not only make the humans using the system more productive, but they also improve the job execution efficiency at a machine level
They eliminate the need for a cluster
They guarantee exactly-once semantics
They provide low-latency query responses

questions.explanation: Interactivity plus machine-level efficiency.

questions.question: What does a cost-based optimizer do for joins?

options.text: Because joins are specified in a declarative way — the application simply states which joins are required and the query optimizer decides how they can best be executed — the framework can analyze the properties of the join inputs and automatically decide which join algorithm would be most suitable for the task at hand. Hive, Spark and Flink have cost-based query optimizers that can do this, and even change the order of joins so that the amount of intermediate state is minimized. The choice of join algorithm can make a big difference to the performance of a batch job, and it is nice not to have to understand and remember all the various join algorithms
It rewrites user-defined functions for speed
It chooses the number of reducers only
No batch framework has a cost-based optimizer

questions.explanation: Declarative specification is what makes automatic algorithm selection possible.

questions.question: How do MapReduce and its successors differ from SQL's fully declarative model, and what does that buy?

options.text: MapReduce and its dataflow successors are very different from the fully declarative query model of SQL. MapReduce was built around the idea of function callbacks: for each record or group of records a user-defined function — the mapper or reducer — is called, and that function is free to call arbitrary code in order to decide what to output. This approach has the advantage that you can draw upon a large ecosystem of existing libraries to do things like parsing, natural language analysis, image analysis, and running numerical or statistical algorithms
They are fully declarative and cannot run arbitrary code
They use a restricted expression language with no callbacks
They differ only in syntax

questions.explanation: The freedom to easily run arbitrary code is what has long distinguished batch processing systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases. Although databases have facilities for writing user-defined functions, they are often cumbersome to use and not well integrated with the package managers and dependency management systems that are widely used in most programming languages — such as Maven for Java, npm for JavaScript and Rubygems for Ruby.

questions.question: Why does even a trivial filter benefit from being declared, and what optimizations does that unlock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because if a callback function contains only a simple filtering condition, or it just selects some fields from a record, then there is significant CPU overhead in calling the function on every record

Columnar reads: if such simple filtering and mapping operations are expressed in a declarative way, the query optimizer can take advantage of column-oriented storage layouts and read only the required columns from disk
Vectorized execution: Hive, Spark DataFrames and Impala use vectorized execution, iterating over data in a tight inner loop that is friendly to CPU caches and avoiding function calls
Code generation: Spark generates JVM bytecode and Impala uses LLVM to generate native code for these inner loops

questions.explanation: By incorporating declarative aspects in their high-level APIs, and having query optimizers that can take advantage of them during execution, batch processing frameworks begin to look more like MPP databases and can achieve comparable performance — while by retaining the extensibility of being able to run arbitrary code and read data in arbitrary formats, they keep their flexibility advantage. As batch processing systems gain built-in functionality and high-level declarative operators, and as MPP databases become more programmable and flexible, the two are beginning to look more alike: in the end, they are all just systems for storing and processing data.

questions.question: Why is extensibility not enough on its own, and which reusable domain implementations does the chapter name?

options.text: Because while the extensibility of being able to run arbitrary code is useful, there are also many common cases where standard processing patterns keep reoccurring, so it is worth having reusable implementations of the common building blocks. Historically MPP databases served the needs of business intelligence analysts and business reporting, but that is just one among many domains in which batch processing is used. Named implementations include Mahout for statistical and numerical algorithms for machine learning, implemented on top of MapReduce, Spark and Flink, and MADlib which implements similar functionality inside a relational MPP database (Apache HAWQ); spatial algorithms such as k-nearest neighbors, which searches for items that are close to a given item in some multi-dimensional space — a kind of similarity search; and approximate search, which is useful for genome analysis algorithms that need to find strings that are similar but not identical
Extensibility is sufficient; no reusable libraries exist
Only Mahout exists, for machine learning
Reusable libraries exist only inside MPP databases

questions.explanation: Three domains with named, reusable implementations.

questions.question: Which design principles does the Summary say MapReduce and dataflow engines inherited from Unix?

options.text: From Unix tools such as awk, grep and sort: that inputs are immutable, that outputs are intended to become the input to another (as yet unknown) program, and that complex problems are solved by composing small tools that 'do one thing well'
That programs should be monolithic, typed and interactive
That data should be modeled up front and validated on write
That outputs should be mutable and reused in place

questions.explanation: Note the parenthetical 'as yet unknown' — the program consuming your output may not exist yet.

questions.question: Give the uniform interface at each layer.

options.text: In the Unix world the uniform interface that allows one program to be composed with another is files and pipes; in MapReduce that interface is a distributed filesystem. Dataflow engines add their own pipe-like data transport mechanisms to avoid materializing intermediate state to the distributed filesystem, but the initial input and final output of a job is still usually HDFS
Unix uses pipes only; MapReduce uses pipes; dataflow engines use files
All three use the same distributed filesystem
Dataflow engines have no uniform interface

questions.explanation: Pipes in the middle, files at the edges.

questions.question: What are the two main problems distributed batch processing frameworks must solve, and how does each system solve them?

options.text: Partitioning: in MapReduce, mappers are partitioned according to input file blocks, and the output of mappers is repartitioned, sorted and merged into a configurable number of reducer partitions — the purpose being to bring all the related data, for example all the records with the same key, together in the same place. Post-MapReduce dataflow engines try to avoid sorting unless it is required, but they otherwise take a broadly similar approach to partitioning. And fault tolerance: MapReduce frequently writes to disk, which makes it easy to recover from an individual failed task without restarting the entire job but slows down execution in the failure-free case; dataflow engines perform less materialization of intermediate state and keep more in memory, which means they need to recompute more data if a node fails, and deterministic operators reduce the amount of data that needs to be recomputed
Replication and compression, solved identically by both
Scheduling and monitoring, solved by YARN in both cases
Encoding and serialization, solved by Avro in both cases

questions.explanation: Partitioning and fault tolerance, with opposite materialization trade-offs.

questions.question: Reproduce the Summary's descriptions of the three join algorithms. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sort-merge joins: each of the inputs being joined goes through a mapper that extracts the join key; by partitioning, sorting and merging, all the records with the same key end up going to the same call of the reducer, which can then output the joined records

Broadcast hash joins: one of the two join inputs is small, so it is not partitioned and can be entirely loaded into a hash table — thus you start a mapper for each partition of the large join input, load the hash table for the small input into each mapper, and then scan over the large input one record at a time, querying the hash table for each record

Partitioned hash joins: if the two join inputs are partitioned in the same way, using the same key, same hash function and same number of partitions, then the hash table approach can be used independently for each partition
These algorithms also provide a good illustration of how partitioned algorithms work, and most of them are also internally used in MPP databases and dataflow engines

questions.explanation: Three algorithms, useful beyond joining as a model of partitioned computation.

questions.question: State the restriction imposed on callback functions and what it buys.

options.text: Distributed batch processing engines have a deliberately restricted programming model: callback functions such as mappers and reducers are assumed to be stateless and to have no externally visible side effects besides their designated output. This restriction allows the framework to hide some of the hard distributed systems problems behind its abstraction — in the face of crashes and network issues tasks can be retried safely, and the output from any failed tasks is discarded; if several tasks for a partition succeed, only one of them actually makes its output visible. Thanks to the framework, your code in a batch processing job does not need to worry about implementing fault-tolerance mechanisms: the framework can guarantee that the final output of a job is the same as if no faults had occurred, even though in reality various tasks perhaps had to be retried. These reliable semantics are much stronger than what you usually have in online services that handle user requests and that write to databases as a side effect of processing a request
Callbacks may be stateful and have side effects, which the framework tracks
The restriction buys only performance, not fault tolerance
There is no restriction on callbacks

questions.explanation: Statelessness and no side effects are what make transparent retry safe.

questions.question: State the defining property of a batch processing job and how Chapter 11 changes the picture.

options.text: The distinguishing feature of a batch processing job is that it reads some input data and produces some output data, without modifying the input — in other words the output is derived from the input. Crucially the input data is bounded: it has a known, fixed size, for example a set of log files at some point in time or a snapshot of a database's contents. Because it is bounded, a job knows when it has finished reading the entire input, and so a job eventually completes when it is done. In the next chapter we turn to stream processing, in which the input is unbounded — you still have a job, but its inputs are never-ending streams of data, so a job is never complete because at any time there may still be more work coming in. Stream and batch processing are similar in some respects, but the assumption of unbounded streams also changes a lot about how we build systems
The defining feature is low latency; Chapter 11 reduces it further
The defining feature is the use of HDFS; Chapter 11 replaces it with Kafka
The defining feature is the map-reduce shape; Chapter 11 generalizes it

questions.explanation: Bounded input is what makes completion meaningful — and losing it is what makes stream processing different.
